issues: The claim overstates what was read. It says 'The published standard names AI agents'. The only text checked is the standard's official abstract, on the IEEE SA page and, identically, on IEEE Xplore. The normative text was not read (the slice notes say so: the GET PDF sits behind IEEE sign-in). The scope sentences read from Xplore metadata speak only of 'organizational entities acting as second-party service providers' and do not mention AI agents. I reworded the claim so it cites the abstract.

Nuance for the page: in the abstract, AI agents are listed as service providers that individuals engage, so they are second-party counterparties. They are not named as the individual's own agent. Agents acting for the parties are covered separately: 'Computing devices and software performing as agents for both first and second parties'. Do not read this sentence as 'the standard provides for personal AI agents'.

addSources.quote: This draft standard covers contractual interactions and agreements between individuals and the service providers they engage on a network, including websites.

issues: No error found. doc.searls.com returns 403 to the helper, so I fetched the page with curl (HTTP 200) on 2026-09-23 into the helper cache and ran --check: FOUND. The title is 'Now We Begin' and the <time datetime> is '2026-01-29T14:40:00-05:00'. The quote is in Searls's 'This is how it works' list, which describes the standard beside a diagram 'that predates the one in the standard, but says the same thing'.

The claim leans on the working-group chair's own summary, so I added a primary source. The IEEE abstract confirms agents on both sides and an open protocol: 'Computing devices and software performing as agents for both first and second parties shall engage using any protocol that serves the purpose.' The abstract does not itself mention AI as the parties' agents. The 'personal and corporate AIs' range is Searls's reading, repeated in his 24 Nov 2025 post ('as simple as browser and server plug-ins, or as complex as AI agents on both sides'). The MyTerms FAQ says 'Both parties use agents, which can be as simple as browser and website add-ons.'
Caution: the abstract also says the agreement 'shall be signed electronically by both parties or their agents'. So agents are how parties may act, not a separate requirement.
